Upgrade the high-load anaerobic digestion and relieve acid stress through 
the strategy of side-stream micro-aeration: biochemical performances, 
microbial response and intrinsic mechanisms 
Wen Li a, Yongli Liu a, Baocun Wu a, Li Gu a,*, Rui Deng b 
a Key laboratory of the Three Gorges Reservoir Region’s Eco-environments, Ministry of Education, Institute of Environment and Ecology, Chongqing University, 174 
Shapingba Road, Chongqing 400045, PR China 
b School of Architecture and Urban Planning, Chongqing Jiaotong University, Chongqing 400074, PR China   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
High-load anaerobic digestion 
Acid stress 
Side-stream micro-aeration 
Metagenomic analysis 
A B S T R A C T   
In high-load anaerobic digestion such as in kitchen waste, side-stream micro-aeration (SMA) shows excellent 
operational performance to direct micro-aeration (DMA). It immediately restores the acidification to stability. 
Methanogenic performance remained stable when organic load ratios (OLR) was further increased to 5.5 g VS/L. 
Enhanced enzyme activity, microbial aggregation, and proliferation of bacteria and archaea were observed in 
SMA. The results indicates that SMA enriched Methanosaeta (relative abundance exceeded 93%) and induced the 
change of the main methanogenic pathway to acetoclastic methanogenesis. Mechanisms was further explored by 
using metagenomic analysis, and the results show SMA avoids mass formation of ROS (reactive oxygen species) 
by cycling the aerated slurry, and retains benefits of trace O2 on material and energic metabolism, which poses 
great application potentials and deserves further investigation.   
1. Introduction 
Urban food waste (FW) is an important part of household waste that 
is rich in nutrients, which can be utilized via anaerobic digestion (AD). 
However, the high proportion of easily biodegradable organic matter in 
FW commonly results in rapid acidification, as well as subsequent 
acidity accumulation in its AD, especially when high feed load is 
applied. The acidity accumulation deteriorates systematic stability by 
inhibiting anaerobic microbes, and if not properly treated, system fail­
ure occurs. However, AD with high organic load ratios (OLR) presents 
the advantage of high volume gas yield and small reactor volume, which 
have great potential for AD-engineered treatment of different kinds of 
organic wastes (Li et al., 2022). Therefore, it is of great significance to 
effectively maintain the stability of such a AD system. Effectively 
diluting the adverse effects of inhibitors during high-load anaerobic 
digestion is a key hurdle. 
Several studies have explored to handle acid inhibition, including the 
use of exogenous alkaline (Chen et al., 2019), cultivating acid-resistant 
strains via pre-inoculation, gradient culture, or using trace elements to 
enhance microbial activity (Zhang and Loh, 2019), and accelerating the 
transfer of electrons from syntrophic oxidation bacteria to methanogens 
through exogenous conductors (Zhao, 2020). In these processes, the 
fundamental goal is to effectively reduce the accumulation of fatty acids, 
such as propionate and butyric acid, which cannot be directly used by 
methanogenic archaea. 
In recent years, micro-aeration has attracted much attention in 
ameliorating these challenges. In such processes, a small amount of air is 
injected into the anaerobic digestive system to induce the fluctuation of 
the digestive ORP (Oxidation Reduction Potential). Trace oxygen acts as 
an electron receptor to capture/shunt excess electrons produced in AD of 
perishable organics, alleviating acid inhibition and promoting meth­
anogenesis. Yu et al.(2020) observed that during AD of black water, an 
appropriate micro-oxygen supply improved hydrolysis, acidification and 
even methanogenic efficiency, and the abundance of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens significantly increased. According to Nguyen et al.(2019), 
intermittent micro-aeration rapidly decreased the total VFA concentra­
tion in the reactor from 9.2 to 3.0 g HAc/L and induced the recovery of 
methane production, thereby improving overall stability of the AD 
system. 
Recently, direct introduction of air into the digester is the most 
common form of intervention used. This kind of micro-aeration is 
impractical for engineering application due to the high cost of full-scale

digesters emptying and reforming, as well as difficulties in assuring the 
homogeneous diffusion of air bubbles to avoid too high ORP in certain 
areas. Compared with direct micro-aeration, side-stream micro-aeration 
(SMA) has great potential for application because micro-aeration can be 
operated in a side-stream reactor with a much smaller volume, which 
avoids heterogeneous diffusion of air in the main digester and lowers the 
potential risks in systems reforming and subsequent operation. Gonza­
lez-Salgado et al. (2020) connected a thermophilic aerobic reactor to 
mesophilic anaerobic digestion by means of a peristaltic recirculation 
pump to circulate the slurry. This side-stream form somewhat increased 
the efficiency of hydrolysis and organics removal. However, research 
about side-stream micro-aeration remains limited, especially in regard 
to performance and mechanism in facing acidity stress. 
Here, the side-stream micro-aeration approach for AD in FW under 
mesophilic conditions is adopt, aiming to relieve acidity stress in order 
to maintain systematic stability under high OLRs. Digestion perfor­
mance under different reactor modes were examined and compared. 
This work focused on the ability of the side-stream micro-aeration to 
relieve acid inhibition. To clarify the mechanism of this kind of micro- 
aeration in relieving acidity stress, we investigated the response and 
feedback of the microbial community structure, as well as the microbial 
metabolic pathway. The results of this study provide new insights and 
reference for improving the stability of overloaded AD systems. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Substrates and inoculum 
Inoculum applied in this study was taken from an anaerobic diges­
tion tank of Tangjiatuo wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) in 
Chongqing, China. The WWTP adopts A2/O process and the treatment 
capacity is about 40,000 t/d. The inoculation sludge was pretreated by 
settling and subsequent filtration through a 20-mesh screen to get pu­
rified and concentrated. The prepared inoculum was stored under 
anaerobic conditions at 35±1 ◦C for more than one week before use to 
reduce background methanation. The substrate used in this work is 
simulated FW to avoid the unnecessary effect of organic fractions’ 
variation on digestive efficiency. The simulated FW is composed by 400 
g rice, 300 g cabbage, 200 g pork and 100 g tofu. These raw materials 
were firstly cooked in distilled water, and then were crushed to assure 
the particle size less than 5 mm. Finally, the crushed slurry was diluted 
to the volume of 2.0 L. Characteristics of the substrates and the inoculum 
are listed in Table S1. 
2.2. Digester set-up and operational conditions 
The side-stream micro-aeration system (SMA) consisted of a main 
digester and a side-stream reactor equipped with aeration devices 
(aerator and gas tube). Their volume were 3.0 and 0.7 L. Schematic 
diagram of the device structure can be found in Fig. S1. The AD system 
was equipped with feed hoppers, a mixing shaft, a separate jacketed 
thermostat, ORP online monitoring, and gas collection devices. Digests 
were excreted from the main reactors. Daily circulation amount of the 
slurry from the main digester to the side-stream reactor accounted for 
18% of the total by referring from previous study (Wu et al., 2016). The 
recirculation was realized by a peristaltic pump with a flow rate of 190 
mL/min. The operation was as follows: 0.7 L of sludge from the 
side-stream reactor was completely transferred to the main reactor and 
mixed thoroughly with the slurry in the main reactor. Another same 
system without aeration devices (SD), as well as a direct micro-aeration 
digester without side-stream reactor (DMA) were also built to provide 
comparison. The experimental design and the analysis performed was 
described in Table S2a. All three AD systems were operated under a 
semi-continuous feeding mode to maintain a constant hydraulic reten­
tion time (HRT) of 20 days and the OLRs ranging from 2.5 to 5.5 g 
VS/L⋅day (shown in Table S2b). The digestive temperature was 
maintained at 35±1 ◦C. According to the OLRs, the experimental process 
can be divided into five stages. In fourth and fifth stage, a little air was 
introduced daily after substrate feeding. The dose was 20 mL and the 
aeration intensity was 0.03L Air/L reactor.d. And this was selected as the 
optimal dose by pre-experiments (Fig. S2). Air was injected into the 
side-stream digester in a feeding-discharge period through a syringe 
over 10 min and the injection process was manually controlled to pro­
ceed uniformly and slowly, resulting in the injection rate of approxi­
mately 2 mL/min. All reactors and experiments were triply operated. 
2.3. Analytical methods 
2.3.1. Chemical and physical analysis 
Measurements of total solid (TS), volatile solid (VS), chemical oxy­
gen demand (COD), alkalinity and NH4
+-N were conducted in accordance 
with standard methods (Gao et al., 2022). pH was determined by pH 
meter (FE28, METTLER TOLEDO, Switzerland). Gasbags were used to 
collect the biogas in the digesters, and the volume was measured by a 
graduated syringe through repeat extracting the gas from the bag. The 
biogas composition and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) were determined by a 
gas chromatography (Jiedao GC1690, Hangzhou). The operation pro­
cess of gas chromatography was introduced in detail in previous study 
(Tian et al., 2021). α-Glucosidase activity, ATP content, coenzyme F420, 
CAT (catalase), as well as acetate kinase were measured by using the 
ELISA kit (Shanghai hengyuan biological technology co., LTD). Electron 
transfer activity (ETS) was measured using the method reported by Wan 
et al. (2016). Quantification of C, H and O elements using an elemental 
analyzer (Elementar Analysensysteme GmbH, Unicube). Confocal laser 
scanning microscope (CLSM) staining and observation was conducted 
according to the method reported by Chen et al. (2007). 
2.3.2. Microbial community and absolute quantitative PCR analyses 
Samples were taken from the raw sludge and SMA digester at the end 
of stage III and IV for microbial analysis. Microbial communities were 
analyzed by high-throughput 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Microbial 
community genomic DNA was extracted using the E.Z.N.A.® soil DNA 
Kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA, U.S.) according to manufacturer’s 
instructions. The hypervariable region V3-V4 of the bacterial 16S rRNA 
gene were amplified with primer pairs 338F(5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGG­
CAGCAG-3′) and 806R(5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′) by an ABI 
GeneAmp® 9700 PCR thermocycler (ABI, CA, USA), the hypervariable 
region V3-V5 of the archaea rRNA gene were amplified with primer 
pairs Arch344F(5′-ACGGGGYGCAGCAGGCGCGA-3′) and Arch915R(5′- 
GTGCTCCCCCGCCAATTCCT-3′). PCR amplification; agarose gelelec­
trophoresis; DNA purification and recovery; and DNA library sequencing 
preparation were all performed according manufacturer’s instructions. 
Operational taxonomic units (OTUs) with 97% similarity cutoff were 
clustered using UPARSE version 7.1, and chimeric sequences were 
identified and removed. The taxonomy of each OTU representative 
sequence was analyzed by RDP Classifier version 2.2 against the 16S 
rRNA database (eg. Silva v138) using confidence threshold of 0.7. 
The absolute content of 16s and ARCH archaeal genes in the samples 
was determined by using Real-time PCR assay, DNA samples prepared 
from the previous step were reacted in a 96-well plate in a fluorescence 
quantitative PCR instrument (Type ABI7300, Applied Biosystems, USA). 
The primers selected for the 16S rRNA gene were Eub338_Eub806, and 
those for the archaeal gene were Arch344F_Arch915R. 
2.3.3. Metagenomic sequencing and analysis 
Using E.Z.N.A.® Soil DNA Kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA, U.S.) to 
extract total genomic DNA of the sample according to the manufac­
turer’s instructions. Concentration and purity of extracted DNA was 
determined with TBS-380 and NanoDrop2000, respectively. DNA 
extract quality was checked on 1% agarose gel. The DNA was broken 
into fragments of approximately 400 bp using ultrasound (Covaris 
M220, USA). Sequencing library was constructed using the NEXTflexTM

Rapid DNA-Seq. Subsequently, Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., 
Ltd. (Shanghai, China) used the Illumina NovaSeq/Hiseq Xten(Illumina 
Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) for sequencing. The raw reads from meta­
genome sequencing were processed on the free online platform of 
Majorbio Cloud Platform (cloud.majorbio.com). 
2.4. Statistical analysis 
An analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed to evaluate the 
significance of results, and if the calculated p was less than 0.05, the 
corresponding result was considered statistically significantly. In this 
study, statistical analysis was conducted by IBM SPSS statistic.

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Digestion performance 
Fig. 1 shows the overall digestion performance with increasing OLR 
from 2.5 to 5.5 g VS/L⋅d and the effects of micro-aeration. Digesters run 
stable when OLR was maintained lower than 4.0 gVS/L⋅d (Stage II). 
When OLR was further increased to 5.0 gVS/L⋅d (Stage III), acid accu­
mulation and subsequent acid inhibition occurred gradually due to 
overload of feeding organics. There is a significant decline in the specific 
methane yield from about 367 mL/gVS at the end of stage II to 339 mL/ 
gVS after several days’ digestion. By the end of stage III, the specific 
methane production was reduced by 33.07% relative to the end of stage 
II. After 20 days’ operation under such OLRs, micro-aeration was 
introduced in the direct (DMA) and side-stream (SMA) modes, and a 
sharp contrast in the digestion performance was observed. There was 
intense acidification in the SD digester with significant decreases of 
methane production (Fig. 1a) and pH values. The VFA concentration 
climbed rapidly (Fig. 1b), while the ratio of VFA/ALK exceeded the 
warning value of 0.3 (Fig. S3), indicating the balance between acidity 
and alkalinity had been eliminated. Direct injection of air into the main 
digester (DMA) further accelerated the acidification, and a steep climb 
in TVFA concentration was observed. These two AD systems (SD and 
DMA) collapsed rapidly. The results for direct air introduction differ 
from previous studies reported by Nguyen et al. (2019) where direct 
micro-aeration restored the acidification in the digester. These differ­
ences may be due to distinct properties of feeding stock substrates. 
Compared to lignocellulosic biomass used by Nguyen et al. (2019), FW 
in this study presents much higher biodegradability, with much higher 
rates of hydrolytic-acidification. Therefore, direct air introduction 
further accelerated acidity accumulation. However, in this study, SMA 
responded opposite to DMA. The AD system showed an immediate 
response and side-stream micro-aeration prevented further decline in 
specific methane production (Fig. 1a), and the methane production 
properties were restored immediately to previous levels with increasing 
CH4 content up to 60.01% (Table 1). Meanwhile, the TVFA concentra­
tion declined gradually restoring the pH of the slurry (Fig. 1b). After 20 
days of the SMA, TVFA concentration decreased from 4.59 to 1.32 g 
HAc/L (Table 1). The lowered TVFA concentration assured the index of 
VFA/ALK ratio was maintained lower than 0.3 (Fig. S3), even at high 
OLR, which guarantees a good environment for methanogens. Also, 
propionate concentration decreased rapidly, while acetate concentra­
tion showed a small increase (Fig. S4). This result can be attributed to 
the conversion of VFA, such as propionate. Guo et al. (2021) also re­
ported that moderate micro-aeration is beneficial to VFA consumption. 
The introduction of SMA prevented the decline of TCOD removal, and 
TCOD removal for the SMA system was maintained at about 69.2% 
(Table 1). These results indicate that the SMA digester was restored to 
stability and can run efficient digestion of FW at high OLRs. 
The above results have shown the potential of SMA to relieve the 
acidity accumulation under high OLR. Therefore, this study further 
increased the OLR from 5.0 to 5.5 gVS/L⋅d (stage V) to explore SMA 
limitations. Specific methane yield further improved to about 330 mL/g 
VS under such OLR, and the methane production performance was 
stable, even at the end of this stage. It is interesting that though total 
VFA concentration in this stage climbed gradually to higher than 3000 
mg HAc/L with the slow decline of pH to below 7.2 (Fig. 1b), the system 
still ran properly. This reflects that SMA improves the tolerance of the 
system and optimizes the operational performance of anaerobic diges­
tion in various aspects. 
Changes to ORP in the SMA and DMA reactors were also recorded 
during a day in stage IV, and the results are shown in Figure S5. The 
application of side-stream micro-aeration brought a slight increase in 
ORP, and the ORP in slurry stabilized gradually to base levels. However, 
in the DMA reactor, a steeper climb and long duration time of the ORP 
was observed. 
3.2. Enzymes activity 
Micro-aeration in AD is believed to promote hydrolytic and fer­
menting microorganisms, so it is necessary to understand the positive 
effects of SMA on hydrolytic-acidification to reveal potential mecha­
nisms. Fig. 2 compares enzyme activity before and after SMA treatment. 
α-glucosidase plays a role in the hydrolysis of polysaccharides (Ruan 
et al., 2019). Increased α-glucosidase activity after aeration was 
involved in the hydrolysis of polysaccharide-like organics. This supports 
the recovery of high levels of methane and organics conversion after 
systemic acid accumulation. Acetate kinase, a key enzyme participating 
in acetate production, increased significantly after aeration. Increased 
activity of α-glucosidase and acetate kinase verified the enhanced 
hydrolytic-acidification process brought by micro-aeration. In addition, 
the ATP content in the system increased significantly after aeration, 
indicating that micro-oxygen promoted the growth and metabolism of 
microorganisms resulting in more microbial activity and hydrolase 
production. For methanogenesis, the activity of F420 declined after 
treatment (p<0.001). F420 is commonly used as an electron donor in the 
reduction of CO2 to CH4, lowered F420 indicates hindered CO2 reduction, 
and it is quite possible that the acetoclastic methanogenesis pathway 
may dominate after SMA treatment (Wunderer et al., 2022). The 
introduction of oxygen created reactive oxygen species (ROS), hence the 
level of CAT was observed a slight increase (Wu et al., 2021). However, 
CAT content remained low, likely due to other mechanisms in SMA, and 
the level of ROS in SMA may not be high.

by monitoring electron transport systems (ETS) during microbial 
metabolism (Fig. 2). Electron transport usually occurs in the cytoplasmic 
membranes of bacteria that generate flavoproteins by coupling the 
oxidation of NADH and other substrates to the protons. In aerobic 
respiration, quinone acts as a hydrogen carrier to transfer electrons to 
appropriate terminal electron acceptors such as O2 producing cyto­
chromes. O2 can easily act as an electron acceptor in ETS, thus 
increasing activity (Wang et al., 2020). After SMA treatment, ETS ac­
tivity in the digester increased significantly by 21%. This increase 
probably stemmed from the fact that trace amounts of oxygen added by 
SMA became the optimal electron acceptor. Notably, cytochromes 
generated by electron transport are important for overcoming oxidative 
stress, which is another way SMA may tolerate ROS. In addition, 
enhanced ETS activity also facilitates metabolism by maintaining redox 
homeostasis, which may contribute to digester stability. 
3.3. Carbon mass balance 
Samples were taken before and after SMA treatment to build carbon 
mass balance (Fig. 3). The carbon contained in the feeding stock was 
dominated by carbohydrates and proteins, which are partly converted to 
biogas and partly used by cells for synthesis. Carbon recovery in the 
form of CH4 can be used to indicate the return of system stability. CH4 
increased from 18.8% in the unstable period (stage III) to 22.0% in stage 
IV after the application of SMA, and methane content in the biogas was 
significantly higher (Table 1). It is worth noting that the system faced 
severe pressure due to high OLR during this period. This finding further 
supports the important role of SMA in maintaining systematic stability. 
Moreover, in stage IV, the proportion of carbon recovered in the form of 
intermediates decreased significantly, while the carbon recovered in the 
form of digestates increased significantly. The decrease of intermediates 
may be ascribed to the enhanced conversion of particulate matter into 
soluble compounds, resulting in the increased carbon content in the 
digestates. The enhanced conversion of particulate organics indicates 
metabolic activity of fermentating bacteria in response to SMA in these 
stages. Combining the results observed in section 3.1 and 3.2, we 
inferred that the introduction of SMA restores the system from collapse 
by converting or consuming SCFA. Additionally, SMA promoted mi­
croorganisms metabolic activity, and thus, the hydrolytic-acidification 
processes were improved providing sufficient intermediates with low 
molecular weight for subsequent methanogenesis. Although the carbon 
balance could not clarify the specific path of carbon flow to methane, the 
conversion of VFA and the changes of key enzymes indicate changes in 
methanogenesis in response to SMA. 
3.4. Microbial analysis 
3.4.1. CLSM 
In the CLSM image, SYTO 63 stains nucleic acids, Con A-AF555 
(Fluorescently labeled lectins Concanavalin A) stains the α-mannopyr­
anosyl and α-glucopyranosyl sugar, FITC (fluorescein isothiocyanate) 
stains proteins and other amine-containing compounds such as amino- 
sugars in the granules, calcofluor white stains β-D-glucopyranose poly­
saccharides, Merged represents the combined image of four dyes. 
Fig. 4 shows the distribution of components in the sludge observed in 
CLSM. According to the fluorescence intensity, a large number of fila­
mentous microorganisms were observed in both samples, and the cells in 
the samples after SMA treatment were more densely distributed tending 
to form tightly aggregated morphology (Fig. 4). In addition, after SMA 
treatment, both polysaccharides (including α-mannose, α-glucose, and 
β-D-glucopyranose polysaccharides) almost cover the area where cells 
were located, while protein only appears in some areas. We speculate 
that the sample forms a tight core, and the glucose polysaccharide ag­
gregates at the outer layer of the cell granules, similar to McSwain 
(2005). This may be related to EPS, which is capable of aggregating 
microorganisms. EPS with polysaccharide, as a skeleton, agglomerates 
microorganisms and organics. This form of a compact whole is favorable 
for electron transfer and metabolic processes. In addition, this form may 
resist the outside adverse environment. It can gather obligate anaerobes 
in the inner space and eliminate the toxic effects of ROS (singlet oxygen 
(1O2), superoxide anion radicals (O2⋅−), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and 
hydroxyl radicals (OH⋅)) (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). Meantime, the

attached antioxidant enzymes and polyphosphate can help cells to

3.4.2. Diversity 
Samples were taken at the end of each stage for microbial analysis. 
Inoculum sludge was also taken for comparison. Indices related to mi­
crobial richness and diversity were analyzed. In general, the level of 
species evenness was proportional to microbial diversity. Higher values 
of Sobs, Ace and Chao indicate higher microbial richness. Shannon and 
Simpson indices are negatively correlated, while a higher Shannon index 
indicates higher microbial uniformity (Xu et al., 2021). In the bacterial 
community, the introduction of SMA was found to resulted in significant 
decreases in both species richness and uniformity (Table 2), implying 
that SMA reduced bacterial diversity. The phenomenon in here may be 
due to that trace oxygen stimulate the growth of facultative bacteria and 
limit the growth of bacteria sensitive to oxygen. Meanwhile, there is also

a huge impact on the metabolic pathways, micro-aeration in side-stream 
reactor may create an environment super suitable for the growth of 
dominant bacteria, so that the ecological niches in the digestive system 
are gradually occupied by them, resulting in the decrease of the di­
versity. In addition, the bacterial diversity in the inoculum was signifi­
cantly higher than in other samples, which can be attributed to the 
efficient digestive environment in the reactor for treating sludge. Simi­
larly, archaea had lower microbial diversity in the SMA sample, 
revealing that the archaea community was purified by the SMA. This 
kind of community may pose much higher activity in converting in­
termediates (acetate and H2) into methane. 
3.4.3. Microbial community structure 
In order to reveal the effect of introducing of SMA on the microbial 
community structure, this work examined the microbial community 
compositions for sludges before and after SMA treatment. Meanwhile, q- 
PCR was used to understand the variation of absolute gene numbers in 
the SMA treatment (Fig. 5). There were significant increases in the copy 
number of target genes in bacteria and archaea after SMA, showing that 
SMA treatment accelerates microbial proliferation. The rate of microbial 
reproduction depends on cell growth and division, which generates a 
strong demand for energy and biosynthesis, since cell division- 
dependent proteases (such as SulA) require ATP to function. Because 
ATP is synthesized only when needed due to thermodynamic con­
straints, the observed increase in ATP content also attests to the activity 
of microbial growth and reproduction (Fig. 2). 
Specific to the composition of the microbial community (Fig. S6a), 
most sequences in SMA were assigned to seven phyla: Firmicutes, 
Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, Spirochaetota, Synergistota, Elusimi­
crobiota, Chloroflexi. Except for Bacteroidota and Spirochaetota, the 
relative abundance of other bacterial phyla was significantly increased 
by SMA, suggesting that these microorganisms are more adapted to the 
environment created by SMA. In fact, the first three dominant bacterial 
phyla in SMA are all reported to be facultative bacteria, often found in 
micro-aerobic fermentation systems (Lim et al., 2014). 
Among them, Firmicutes became the dominant bacteria after SMA 
treatment. It has been reported that Firmicutes are important hydrolytic- 
acidifying bacteria with resistance to high temperature and low pH 
(Pervin et al., 2013). Its high abundance explains the higher efficiency in 
organics hydrolysis and subsequent acidification. Actinobacteriota were 
the second dominant bacteria that play an important role in degradation 
of organic matter and forming humus (Zhang et al., 2012). They favor 
sludge aggregation and tend to form stable coated agglomeration par­
ticle structures, which explain the changes in microbial morphology 
observed in Section 3.3.1. Synergistota are able to accelerate the con­

increased abundance is thought to be the key to resolving excessive 
acidity (Ruan et al., 2019). The Synergistota in SMA accelerates the 
consumption of VFA by converting them to acetate that can be further 
used by methanogens. The improved absolute and relative abundance of 
the above bacteria in SMA implies a cooperation among hydrolysis, 
acidification, and subsequent acetate production in AD. Elusimicrobiota 
contained a single, facultative species with a cluster of oxygen stress 
protection genes (Guo et al., 2021), and its proliferation may explain the 
increase in CAT content. Both Chloroflexi and Actinobacteriota can 
degrade complex substrates by producing hydrolysis enzymes (Zigan­
shin et al., 2013). Bacteroidota, which contain hydrolytic and 
acid-producing bacteria involved in the hydrolysis of complex poly­
saccharides (Guo et al., 2014), was slightly reduced after SMA treat­
ment. Spirochaetota are obligate anaerobes whose relative abundance

domestication effect. Methanosaeta is an obligate acetatoclastic metha­
nogen that produces CH4 by direct acetate decomposition. The highest 
abundance in the SMA participated stage indicates that aceticlastic 
methanogenesis is its main methanogenesis pathway, this is also sup­
ported the enzyme results. In addition, other enriched archaea found in 
the SMA reactors were Methanomicrobiales, Methanobacterium, and 
Methanoculleus. Methanobacterium is highly associated with hydrotropic 
methanogenesis and can enhance interspecies H2 transfer during AD 
(Zheng et al., 2021), Methanoculleus are hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogens, which are capable of producing CH4 by reducing CO2 with H2 or 
formate as an electron donor (Dong et al., 2022). The low relative 
abundance of these hydrogenotrophic methanogens explains why H2 
was barely detected throughout the digestive process. In AD of perish­
able organics under high OLR, with the fast formation of VFA, quantities 
of electrons were released and combined with protons to produce H2, 
which needs hydrogenotrophic methanogens to be consumed to ensure 
syntrophic oxidation to convert propionic and butyric acid into acetate. 
SMA reduced H2 generation by accelerating its consumption by intro­
ducing O2. The lower hydrogen partial pressure eliminated the ther­
modynamic barrier in syntrophic oxidation, resulting in fast conversion 
of accumulated VFA into acetate, thus inducing acetoclastic 
methanogens. 
Methanogenesis in SMA differs from previous direct micro-aeration. 
According to previous studies, oxygen directly stimulates facultative 
anaerobes, and the micro-aerobic environment screens out methanogens 
intolerant to oxygen. Due to higher tolerance of hydrotropic metha­
nogens such as Methanobacterium and Methanoculleus, their abundance 
was higher under direct micro-aeration. However, in this study, ROS in 
SMA were weakened in the cycle, which favors the role of Methanosaeta. 
Methanosaeta is sensitive to oxygen but has an advantage in metabolism, 
similar to its higher abundance in reactors with low oxygen (Guo et al., 
2021). In addition, intermediates, energy and ATP still play a role, 
which gives Methanosaeta a more significant advantage in SMA. This is 
the reason for the formation of the unique methanogenic pathway in 
SMA. 
3.5. Metagenomic analysis 
In order to identify the potential mechanisms for the heightened 
performance of high-load AD and the reduction of acid inhibition under 
SMA, this study sampled the genes involved in the metabolic processes 
at the end of stages III and IV to analyze them using macrogenomics, 
while annotating genes and key KEGG pathways (Fig. 6a). Metabolic 
pathways were reconstructed manually in order to gain a comprehensive 
understanding of metabolic processes (Fig. 6b). 
3.5.1. Conversion and utilization of organic compounds 
The KEGG pathways were significantly different under SMA (Fig. 6a 
and Table S3). Most of the key KEGG pathways detected in the samples 
were up-regulated, which is consistent with enhanced anaerobic diges­
tion performance (Fig. 1a). Pathways associated with carbohydrate 
metabolism showed a significant increases, which explains rapid VFA 
depletion (Fig. 1b) and the subsequent gradual recovery to systematic 
stability. 
The Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway (EMP) is the main pathway 
of glucose catabolism, where pyruvate is the final product. The expres­
sion of key genes in this process is shown in Table S4. The expression of 
pfkA/pfk was the highest, using ATP to phosphorylate F-6-P to F-6-bP 
(FBP, Fructose bisphosphate), which belongs to the glycolytic pathway. 
In addition, pfk is a suppressor gene of gluconeogenesis, and another 
suppressor gene pyk was also highly expressed after SMA treatment. pgk 
was most significantly upregulated after SMA treatment. It is involved in 
the conversion of 1,3-Diphosphoglycerate and the generation of ATP 
from ADP. Its activation was reported to be dependent on the catabolic 
control protein (CcpA, K02529), a global regulator that inhibits multiple 
catabolic manipulators involved in the secondary metabolism of carbon 
(Xiao et al., 2021). Ppdk was also highly expressed after SMA treatment, 
and it is involved in the interconversion of pyruvate and phosphoenol­
pyruvate (PEP). Since one glucose can be converted into two PEP mol­
ecules in the EMP pathway, whereas pyk can only convert one PEP to one 
pyruvate, a sudden increase in the upstream reaction activates ppdk 
which is then responsible for catalyzing the reversible conversion of 
PEP, AMP and PPi to pyruvate, ATP and P (Cui et al., 2020). The 
expression of these genes demonstrate that SMA optimizes the balance 
of interconnected nodes in organic transformation and enhances the 
efficiency of favorable transformation processes. 
The pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) is another glucose oxidizing 
pathway, and some of its products can re-enter the EMP. PPP was found 
to play an important role in maintaining systematic stability after SMA 
treatment. Non-oxidative PPP synthesizes key precursors such as amino 
acids, nucleotides, and co-factors, and contributes to the maintenance of 
glycolytic fluxes (Rashida, 2021). PPP was significantly enhanced in 
SMA (Table S4). In addition, non-oxidative PPP can direct the products 
of oxidative PPP (R5P) into glycolysis, which helps maintain NADPH 
levels. This result verifies that SMA stimulates the interconnection be­
tween PPP and glycolysis. The reversibility of non-oxidative PPP helps 
the system achieve dynamic balance via intermediates. 
Amino acid metabolism is coupled with PPP, which is also shown to 
be enhanced by SMA. Glycine, serine and threonine metabolism path­
ways were significantly enhanced (Fig. 6a). The serine family is syn­
thesized via 3-phosphoglycerate and regulated by it, and the metabolism 
of the serine family can promote EMP. The serine family is usually 
converted to pyruvate by deamination and can contribute to the TCA 
cycle through pyruvate and acetyl-CoA (Ye et al., 2018), which is 
important for organic matter conversion and energy metabolism. 
The above results suggest that SMA promotes both carbohydrate and 
amino acid metabolism. The enhanced conversion and utilization of 
organics induced by SMA allows cells to produce sufficient ATP/energy, 
accumulate biomass, and maintain growth, which enhances the ability 
of microorganisms to cope with environmental stress. 
3.5.2. SCFA conversion 
Different fermentation processes have different abilities to oxidize 
NADH and produce H2 and ATP. To avoid the accumulation of large 
amounts of NADH from oxidative dehydrogenation of substrates and to 
maintain the NADH/NAD+ balance, the production of acetate is usually 
accompanied by other products (e.g propionic acid, butyric acid or 
ethanol). The conversion of acetyl-CoA to butyric acid has been reported 
to consume two molecules of NADH (Cheng et al., 2020). Therefore, fast 
conversion of acetyl-CoA avoids the accumulation of NADH that would 
enhance the accumulation of FAs, especially in high OLR AD. SMA 
showed a rapid response to alleviate SCFA accumulation with a signif­
icant upregulation of the fatty acid oxidation pathway (Fig. 6a). The 
involved enzymes are presented in Table S5. 
This work constructed a complete β-oxidation pathway for butyric 
acid metabolism. The most pronounced upregulation of buk (1.70-fold 
promotion) activates butyrate to butyryl-CoA, and another enzyme 
involved in this process, atoD, was also actively expressed (1.67-fold 
promotion) with one ATP synthesized per butyrate molecule in this step 
(Hao et al., 2020). Most atoD originates from Firmicutes, confirming 
their increased abundance (Fig. S6a). AtoB is the most strongly 
expressed enzyme in SMA and is responsible for the final step in pro­
ducing acetyl-CoA. The upregulation of atoB contributes to the distri­
bution of precursors in the acetyl-CoA branch node and is essential for 
the conversion of butyrate to acetate (Kim et al., 2018). In addition, the 
greatest downregulation was observed in fadR, which is involved in the 
oxidation to acetoacetyl-CoA via (S)-3-Hydroxybutanoyl-CoA. fadR is a 
multifunctional regulatory gene that negatively regulates fatty acid 
degradation by reducing the transcription of the fad structural gene 
(Sun et al., 2020). Its downregulation further verifies that fatty acid 
degradation was enhanced in SMA.

in much higher abundance than other enzymes. SMA strongly catalyzed

enzyme involved in the conversion of succinyl-CoA, which is an inter­

to accumulate succinyl-CoA. 
Furthermore, the enhanced conversion of propionic and butyric acid 
reflects enhanced syntrophic oxidation to the production of acetate. 
Pyruvate is an important node in acetate conversion (Table S5). The 
gene for the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA (K03737) also showed 
significant upregulation, while por and nifJ were the most abundant 
enzymes in all relevant metabolic processes. The process of transforming 
pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is essential for metabolism and energy produc­
tion. In addition, electrons (e−) released from oxidized pyruvate are 
transferred via flavodoxin to various reductases that overcome oxidative 
stress and restore the reducing environment in the cell (Nakayama et al., 
2013). 
3.5.3. Methanogenesis 
Both the microbial community analysis (Fig. S6b) and the efficient 
conversion of VFA to acetate suggest that acetoclastic methanogenesis 
dominates methane production. According to the KEGG database, three 
methanogenic pathways exist, including hydrogen, acetate and methyl 
nutrient pathways (Table S6). Fig. S7 shows the genes encoding the 
acetate pathway dominating after SMA treatment with very low 
expression of the hydrogen and methylotrophic pathways. This result is 
consistent with the results of related enzymes (Fig. 2). 
In the acetoclastic pathway, acetate can be converted to acetyl-CoA 
via two ways. The enzymes involved in both processes were highly 
expressed. The abundance of the coding gene for acs was high; it has 
been reported that among C2-C5 short chain fatty acids, acs preferen­
tially utilized acetate with similar affinity (Fujino et al., 2001). The 
activation of this enzyme may be responsible for the increased acetate 
utilization. Also, Methanosaeta has been shown to use acetyl-CoA syn­
thetase to convert acetate (Smith and Ingram-Smith, 2007), which ex­
plains the proliferation of Methanosaeta (Fig. 5). 
The hydrotropic methanogenesis is an important process in previous 
micro-aeration studies, but it was not highly expressed in SMA. The 
small amount of hydrogen methanogenesis in SMA is responsible for 
converting excess H produced by metabolism. The most highly 
expressed enzymes in this pathway, fmd, and specifically fmdE, were 
reported to be closely associated with Methanobacterium (Zheng et al., 
2021), which is consistent with CO2-using methanogens that was found 
in the archaeal community structure (Fig. S6b). The results further 
verifies the differences between DMA and SMA in terms of the archaea 
community and metabolism. 
3.5.4. Energy metabolism 
Due to the introduction of O2 into the anaerobic environment, cells 
should first use O2 as an electron acceptor because it is more favorable in 
thermodynamics, and microorganisms are able to adapt their meta­
bolism pathways from anaerobic to micro-aerobic. The transition of the 
metabolism is accompanied by the changes in energy acquisition. En­
ergy metabolism exhibits a more aerobic-like structure with increased 
levels of oxidative phosphorylation, TCA, and PPP (Table S7). 
Under micro-aerobic conditions, acetyl-CoA undergoes the TCA 
cycle and is further oxidized to CO2 using the electron carrier NADH. 
The proton flow in NADH conversion drives ATP production through 
oxidative phosphorylation to support microorganism growth meta­
bolism. Pyruvate entering the TCA cycle under micro-aerobic conditions 
provides eight times more ATP than that produced by substrate-level 
phosphorylation under anaerobic conditions (Nguyen and Khanal, 
2018). In this study, SMA stimulated key enzymes in the TCA cycle 
including gltA, IDH1-3 and korA. Among them, gltA is the first step in the 
entry of acetyl-CoA into the TCA cycle and competes with other trans­
formations of acetyl-CoA (Tovilla-Couti˜no et al., 2020). The upregula­
tion of gltA and IDH1-3, and the increased expression of korA during 
TCA. This suggests that SMA has potential for microorganisms to un­
dergo a complete TCA cycle providing more energetic support for the 
proliferation of microorganisms. 
Oxidative phosphorylation is another important source of energy for 
the cell. When H+ from carbohydrate metabolism is transferred to the 
hydrogen acceptor NAD via a membrane-associated proton-trans­
locating ATPase, energy containing proton motive force (Δp) can be 
used to generate ATP (Nolfi-Donegan et al., 2020). Significant expres­
sion or upregulation of quinone oxidoreductase (M00144), succinate 
dehydrogenase (M00149), fumarate reductase (M00150) and cyto­
chrome c oxidase (M00154) in SMA is the main manifestation of the 
enhanced 
oxidative 
phosphorylation. 
However, 
electron 
transport-dependent complexes I, III and IV are sources of ROS. How­
ever, under high NADH/NAD+ conditions, O2⋅−production is positively 
upregulated (Murphy, 2009). Thus, SMA promotes microbial growth 
and metabolism in favor of avoiding NADH accumulation, which would 
reduce ROS stress. 
In addition, ppx, a key enzyme in the metabolism of the high energy 
storage substance polyphosphate (polyP), was also observed to be highly 
expressed after SMA treatment. ppx releases the phosphate group at the 
end of the polyP chain which releases a large amount of energy, and its 
involvement also explains the high cellular yield after SMA treatment, 
demonstrating that the energy inherent in polyphosphate and PPi is 
efficiently utilized. 
3.5.5. Oxidative stress regulation 
The micro-aerobic environment created by SMA acts directly on the 
side-stream reactor. After slurry circulation, the ROS formed decays, and 
most microorganisms in the main reactor receive limited stimulation, 
resulting in oxidative stress regulation in the system. 
First, in SMA, polyP, a macromolecular chain polymer and its asso­
ciated enzymes, present an important regulatory role in facing oxidative 
stress. Under extreme conditions, the cellular self-protection mechanism 
centered on polyP is mobilized to promote the formation of a biofilm as a 
protective barrier against hydrogen peroxide (Tunpiboonsak et al., 
2010). This explains the upregulation of lipopolysaccharide and 
peptidoglycan-related gene expression (Fig. 6a). In addition, polyP acts 
as a protein chaperone and resists oxidative stress by preventing protein 
denaturation through translated polyphosphorylation, which occurs by 
a non-enzymatic mechanism (Gray et al., 2014). The identification of 
PPK and other enzymes involved in polyP metabolism in SMA also 
demonstrates that polyP facilitates oxidative stress regulation. In addi­
tion, the increase in CAT (Fig. 2) was evidenced by the upregulation of 
K03386 (peroxiredoxin). The high expression of K04564 (superoxide 
dismutase) also demonstrates the regulatory process of oxidative stress. 
SodA and SodB protect DNA and proteins from oxidative damage by ROS 
(Wu et al., 2021). A two-component regulatory system controls cyo and 
cyd. The expression of cyd was higher in SMA (1.86-fold) because cyd has 
high affinity and is more adapted to low oxygen concentration. In 
addition, anaerobic bacteria can use NADH oxidase to eliminate the 
effects of oxygen, and one of the enzymes observed in SMA, fprA1_2, can 
catalyze the reduction of oxygen to H2O (Hillmann et al., 2009). Upre­
gulation of the superoxide reductase system, which occurs in anaerobic 
bacteria, was also observed. Superoxide reductase dfx reduces super­
oxide to hydrogen peroxide without forming molecular oxygen. This 
system has a coordinated role with NADH oxidase (Jenney et al., 1999).

The expression of oxidative stress-related genes was upregulated in 
SMA, but their expression was low relative to other genes involved in 
metabolism. The antioxidant function performed by anaerobic bacteria 
still occupied a large proportion. This phenomenon supports the hy­
pothesis that a microbial community dominated by facultative anaer­
obes was formed in the side-stream reactor to overcome ROS. More 
importantly, O2 was fully utilized in the side-stream reactor to promote 
energy metabolism to produce associated products. These products were 
exchanged within the system through circulation. The main reactor 
forms a microbial community dominated by anaerobes, complementing 
NADH oxidase to scavenge the remaining ROS and using the favorable 
substances provided by the side-stream reactor. In other words, SMA 
treatment simultaneously limited the negative impacts and improved 
the ability of microorganisms to cope with stress, which may also be the 
main reason why SMA is superior to SD and DMA. 
3.6. Overall summary 
SMA ensured stable performance of the digester under high OLR, 
with more prominent acid-relieving inhibition and better tolerance to 
ROS. Environmental stress brought by SMA profoundly reshaped the 
microbial community structure, causing a dramatic shift in metabolic 
pathways. At the same time, enhanced metabolism maintained cell 
proliferation, which facilitated rapid adaptation to high OLR and 
oxidative stress, eventually restoring system stability (Fig. 7). 
Specifically, SMA treatment enhanced the dominant species of hy­
drolytic acidifying bacteria such as Firmicutes, Actinobacteriota and 
Methanosaeta, and enhanced hydrolysis, fermentation, and methano­
genesis. First, SMA enhanced the conversion and utilization of organic 
matter by promoting EMP, PPP, and amino acid metabolism, and 
enhanced electron shunting from SCFA to acetate. In addition, trace 
oxygen provided by SMA optimized the pathway of energy metabolism, 
and the slurry circulation operation fully exchanged metabolic in­
termediates, related key enzymes, and ATP to meet the material and 
energy requirements for cell proliferation. Meanwhile, SMA effectively 
mitigates the detriment of ROS and facilitates the stable operation of the 
system. 
In conclusion, SMA-based mesophilic anaerobic digestion is a 
promising strategy for high-load, easily hydrolyzed substrates. Because 
SMA can withstand higher OLR, it can efficiently utilize resources and 
reduce the building footprint, generating greater economic benefits. The 
process of SMA inherits the advantage of conventional micro-aeration, 
while the structure avoids the negative effects of ROS and maximizes 
the benefits of micro-aeration, which helps large-scale promotion. 
However, there are still many problems need to be solved in scaling up. 
System controlling would be the first problem. Comprehensive com­
puter program control system needs to be developed to control the 
transportation of slurry from each other, as well as the intensity and 
duration of micro-aeration, by referring the results of online ORP, water 
level, and air flow rate monitoring. Additionally, relatively strong 
mixing is required in the side-stream reactor to assure the heterogeneous 
diffusion of air, which may require excessive electric energy. However, 
the mixing in the side-stream reactor is only needed in the micro- 
aeration period. In a word, there is still a long way to achieve real 
practical application. 
4. Conclusions 
SMA is a promising strategy for maintaining systematic stability in 
AD of high-loaded, easily-hydrolyzed substrates. SMA promoted hy­
drolysis, acidification, and methanogenesis processes and improved 
digestion performance. The participation of trace oxygen in SMA
